name: Sonjo
catalog_citation: Nurse, Derek & Franz Rottland. 1991/92. Sonjo: description, classification, history. Sprache und Geschichte in Afrika (SUGIA) 12/13: 171-289. Köln: Rüdiger Köppe.
catalog_locator: Sec. 2 Phonology, 2.1.2 'Tones', pp. 174-175 (running head 'SONJO: DESCRIPTION, CLASSIFICATION, HISTORY 175' at the page break) and footnote 4 to that section;…
catalog_quote: 2.1.2 Tones Sonjo is a pitch accent language. We had access only to two fairly short tape recordings, neither of which was primarily intended to elicit [4] suprasegmentals. They did not enable us to work out the pitch system. Rather than mark phonetic pitch on some items, and not others, we have chosen not to mark it at all. [fn. 4:] ... one H, which would suggest that Sonjo has pitch accent, rather than tone. Words which are all low in Common Bantu have a H on the first stem syllable in Sonjo: mobélé 'body' (the second H is probably an echo), negégo 'it is a tooth', etc. Words with HL in Common Bantu mostly have H on the prefix: né:guha 'it is a bone', etc. Where the prefix is not syllabic, there is a ... tendency for the H to be heard on the copula: né:ngkɔl' 'it is a heart'. A very small number of words have final H when prepausal: ne losayá 'it is a jaw'. From the very few examples …

new_statements.rule_in_words: The authors classify Sonjo/Temi as a pitch accent (not tone) language: words in their recordings carry (at most) one H, whose position is lexically/etymologically determined -- on the first stem syllable in words that were all-Low in Common Bantu, on the noun-class prefix in words that were *HL (with a further case when the prefix is non-syllabic, cut off in the snippet). They could not work out the system from two short recordings and leave pitch unmarked. Nothing is said about stress; no fixed accent position is claimed.
new_statements.exceptions: A second H in mobélé 'body' is treated as 'probably an echo'; *HL words 'mostly' have H on the prefix; a separate (truncated) statement covers words whose prefix is not syllabic. Authors stress the data limitation (two short tape recordings not designed for suprasegmentals).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (isolated nouns/copular forms such as negégo 'it is a tooth', né:guha 'it is a bone'); based on tape recordings, not systematic elicitation; vowel length also not recorded in the sources although E50 relatives have contrastive length (sec. 2.1.1).
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes 'Sonjo' (the Maasai exonym) = Temi/Ketemi, Glottolog temi1247, ISO soz, Guthrie E46; same language, no dialect specified (authors state the extent of dialect variation within Sonjo is not known). Data are second-hand lexica reinterpreted to 7 vowels plus two short tape recordings.
